Note::argsort¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::argsort(bool descending = false, bool stable = true) const

Return Positions Instead Of Moving Values¶

argsort() returns the linear positions that would arrange a scalar or vector Note in value order. The result is always a rank-one Int64 Note: applying it with take performs the actual reordering while preserving the receiver’s dtype.

Use argsort() when positions matter independently of values: carrying the same permutation into another aligned object, retaining an original-to-sorted mapping, or inspecting where equal values came from. Use sort when only the reordered Note is needed. sort(dim) supports matrix and rank-three lanes; this argsort() overload intentionally accepts only rank zero and rank one because it returns one unambiguous linear permutation and has no axis parameter.

Parameters And Ordering¶

Parameter

Meaning

Default

descending

Reverse the value order.

false

stable

Preserve original position order among equivalent values.

true

Ordering depends on the homogeneous receiver dtype:

Dtype

Ascending order

Text

exact unsigned UTF-8 byte sequence; no collation, case folding, or normalization

Bytes

exact unsigned byte sequence, including embedded zero bytes

Bool

false before true

Int64

signed integer order

Float64

numeric values in ascending order, followed by NaNs

Descending reverses the value classes, so Float64 NaNs precede numeric values. NaNs are equivalent to one another for ordering; with stable=true, multiple NaN positions retain their input order. Signed zeros compare as equivalent.

With stable=false, equal values may appear in any relative order. The output is still a valid permutation, but code must not rely on tie positions. This mode can avoid stability bookkeeping in the sorting implementation.

The receiver is never copied or rearranged. The method allocates numel() contiguous Int64 positions and sorts those positions while reading receiver lanes. Its memory cost is O(n) and comparison cost is O(n log n) for n values. Text and Bytes comparisons borrow the packed arena; they do not copy cell payloads.

Example 1: Stable Ascending Positions¶

const auto words = pluss::note::make({"b", "a", "b", ""});
std::cout << pluss::note::print(words.argsort()) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, dtype=Int64)
[3, 1, 0, 2]

The empty string is first, then "a". The equal "b" values retain positions 0, 2 because stability is enabled by default.

Example 2: Apply The Permutation Without Leaving Note¶

const auto words = pluss::note::make({"b", "a", "b", ""});
const auto order = words.argsort();
std::cout << pluss::note::print(words.take(order)) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["", "a", "b", "b"]

order is an Int64 Note and take() accepts it directly. No standard-library index vector or numeric Series is required.

Example 3: Descending Stable Order¶

const auto words = pluss::note::make({"b", "a", "b", ""});
std::cout << pluss::note::print(words.argsort(true, true)) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, dtype=Int64)
[0, 2, 1, 3]

The duplicate positions remain 0, 2; only value-class order reverses.

Example 4: Request Unstable Sorting When Ties Do Not Exist¶

const auto words = pluss::note::make({"delta", "alpha", "charlie", "bravo"});
std::cout << pluss::note::print(words.argsort(false, false)) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, dtype=Int64)
[1, 3, 2, 0]

With unique values, stability cannot affect the observable permutation.

Example 5: Raw Bytes Use Unsigned Byte Order¶

const auto raw = pluss::note::bytes(
    std::vector<std::string>{"\xFF", "\x01", "\x7F"},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 1>{3});
std::cout << pluss::note::print(raw.argsort()) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[3], dim=1, numel=3, dtype=Int64)
[1, 2, 0]

The leading bytes are 0x01, 0x7F, and 0xFF; no text decoding occurs.

Example 6: Bool And Int64 Ordering¶

std::cout << "Bool\n"
          << pluss::note::print(
                 pluss::note::make({true, false, true, false}).argsort())
          << '\n';
std::cout << "Int64\n"
          << pluss::note::print(
                 pluss::note::make(
                     std::vector<std::int64_t>{10, -2, 10, 0}).argsort())
          << '\n';

Output¶

Bool
Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, dtype=Int64)
[1, 3, 0, 2]
Int64
Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, dtype=Int64)
[1, 3, 0, 2]

Stability keeps the two false positions and the two integer-10 positions in their original relative order.

Example 7: Float64 NaN Placement¶

#include <limits>

const auto values = pluss::note::make(std::vector<double>{
    2.0, std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN(), -1.0,
    std::numeric_limits<double>::quiet_NaN()});

std::cout << "ascending\n" << pluss::note::print(values.argsort()) << '\n';
std::cout << "descending\n"
          << pluss::note::print(values.argsort(true, true)) << '\n';

Output¶

ascending
Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, dtype=Int64)
[2, 0, 1, 3]
descending
Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, dtype=Int64)
[1, 3, 0, 2]

Ascending places -1, then 2, then both NaNs. Descending places the stable NaN pair first, followed by 2 and -1.

Example 8: Scalar And Empty Results Are Still Vectors¶

std::cout << "scalar\n"
          << pluss::note::print(pluss::note::make("scalar").argsort()) << '\n';
std::cout << "empty\n"
          << pluss::note::print(
                 pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::string>{}).argsort())
          << '\n';

Output¶

scalar
Note(shape=[1], dim=1, numel=1, dtype=Int64)
[0]
empty
Note(shape=[0], dim=1, numel=0, dtype=Int64)
[]

A scalar has one ordering position, 0. An empty vector has the unique empty permutation.

Example 9: Invalid Rank And Absence Reject¶

try {
  (void)pluss::note::make({"b", "a", "d", "c"})
      .reshape({2, 2}).argsort();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) { std::cout << "matrix: rejected\n"; }

try { (void)pluss::Note::undefined().argsort(); }
catch (const pluss::Error&) { std::cout << "undefined: rejected\n"; }

Output¶

matrix: rejected
undefined: rejected
